title: Words Build Workplaces
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that managers manage in language, and that common corporate phrases such as imposter syndrome, culture fit and single throat to choke quietly shrink teams by blaming individuals, filtering out difference and designing for blame. She explains why these words stick: they are short, vague, status-preserving and baked into templates. Her answer is a ten-point manifesto for behaviour-first leadership that swaps labels for observable behaviour, looks at the system before the person, pairs accountability with support and retires combat metaphors and euphemisms. She adds a simple formula, Behaviour + Context + Impact + Next steps, for describing a situation without judgement. The piece closes with a micro-plan a leader can start next Monday, including retiring five phrases and patching review and hiring templates. The move is to treat vocabulary as a leadership lever that changes decisions, not as word-policing.
points: Leadership language is not neutral: labels like culture fit or imposter syndrome locate the problem in the person and protect the system from scrutiny.
The Behaviour + Context + Impact + Next steps formula replaces labels with observable facts and turns judgement conversations into action plans.
Accountability only counts when paired with real resources, decision rights and a review cadence.
Replacing resistance to change with unresolved risks reframes dissent as a service and rewards people who raise problems early.
A practical Monday plan: retire five phrases, patch review and hiring templates, and give the team a reset question, Can we put that in behaviour terms?
quotes: We don’t manage in a vacuum; we manage in language. The words we use become the water people swim in - subtle cues about safety, status and what “good” looks like.

Imposter syndrome” tells individuals they’re the problem instead of fixing norms and sponsorship. “Culture fit” filters out difference and calls it quality. “Single throat to choke” designs for blame, not collaboration.
Ask what incentives or policy make a behaviour rational. Before calling someone “unreliable”, consider: “Two teams share this role; priorities clash on Tuesdays - we need to fix the handover first.
Commitments are real when resources, authority and a review cadence are real too. You can’t ask people to improve if the support structure isn’t there.
To be clear, this isn’t word-policing. This is an open invitation to check ourselves so we can have better, more productive relationships at work.

Name what happened; where/under what constraints; why it matters; and what you’ll try next. This works because it replaces labels with observable facts, surfaces system causes and moves the conversation from judgement to action.
We don’t have to wait for HR or a rebrand to fix things. We can start small, make our changes visible and our team will follow.
